---
title: "Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means"
---

[Lecture slides](../lectures/07-import/lec.qmd) · [Weekly self-check](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

We have lengths from 24 seedlings. Twelve independently potted plants were
randomly assigned to a control group and twelve to a treatment group. Each plant
was measured at the beginning and end of the same observation period. Can we
bring the measurements into R without losing their meaning?

Open `introcomputing.Rproj` in the extracted course folder. Its `data/` subfolder
contains the supplied files and a `README.md` explaining them. A **CSV** is a
text file in which commas separate columns. Its first line is a header naming
those columns. The file is storage; importing creates an R object in memory.

## Start from a known place

Create `day07.R` in the project root. Run:

```{r}
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
```

`getwd()` reports R's working directory. It should be your extracted project
folder, not the `data` folder. The second line should return `TRUE`. The relative
path `data/seedlings.csv` means “inside data, find seedlings.csv, starting here”.
Your full home-folder path differs from a classmate's; this relative path can
stay the same when they open their own project.

If `file.exists()` returns `FALSE`, inspect the folder in the file manager. A
common problem is opening the ZIP rather than an extracted project, or an extra
folder layer. Avoid solving this by inserting your personal absolute path into
every line of code. Open the correct project instead.

## Import and inspect

The `readr` package provides a table importer. Packages add functions to R;
installing a package puts it on disk, while `library()` loads it for this session.
The [software setup page](../intro/r-rstudio.qmd) explains installation. Loading is needed again after
restarting R.

```{r}
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)
```

`read_csv()` returns a table, displayed as a **tibble**. `head()` shows its first
rows, not the complete dataset. `dim()` gives 24 rows and 4 columns. `names()`
returns column names. `str()` describes structure and types: `plant_id` and
`treatment` are text; the two lengths are numeric. Suppressing the type message
with `show_col_types = FALSE` does not remove the need to check types.

Read the first row aloud: plant P01 is in the control group; its initial length
was 25.7 mm and its final length 44.3 mm. Each **row** represents one plant, each
**column** one variable. Two lengths from the same row are measurements on the
same plant, not two independent plants.

```{r}
seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)
```

`$` selects a named column from the table, giving a vector. The length is 24. A
mean without a unit is incomplete: the average initial length is measured in mm.
The numbers cannot tell you whether the file used mm or cm; the dictionary and
measurement protocol provide that information.

## Missing is different from zero

A missing measurement is represented by `NA` after import. `NA` means not
available. It does not mean zero length, no growth, or a control treatment.

```{r}
example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)
```

The first mean is `NA`: R will not silently pretend all measurements are known.
The second is 15 mm, calculated from two observed values. `na.rm = TRUE` requests
omitting missing values for this calculation. A report must still explain how
many observations were missing and why, if known.

## Your practical

1. Import `seedlings.csv` and save the import and inspection commands in `day07.R`.
2. Record in comments the row count, column count, column meanings, and units.
3. Inspect `tail(seedlings)` to see the last rows. Find P24 and its treatment.
4. Use `sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))` to count missing final measurements.
5. Import `data/leaf-mass.csv` into `leaves`, inspect it, and use its dictionary
   to explain what one row represents. Do not assume it has the seedling columns.
6. Restart R and run your script from the top. The raw CSV files should remain
   exactly as supplied.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: a function is not found

Run `library(readr)` before `read_csv()`. If loading fails because the package is
not installed, use the setup instructions or ask for help. For column names,
copy from `names(seedlings)`; `initial_mm` and `initial` are different names.
:::


## Extended practical — inspect an unfamiliar table systematically

Allow about 90 minutes. A copied import line is not enough to establish that the
right data arrived with the right meaning. Create `day07-inspection.R` and use
it to investigate the new `data/seedlings-transfer.csv`. This simulated study
has 18 independently potted seedlings, nine randomly assigned to control and
nine to treated. Initial and final lengths are millimetres, measured seven days
apart. Each row is one plant, not one independent measurement occasion.

1. Open the course project, print `getwd()`, and check the relative input path
   with `file.exists()`. Import into a new object called `transfer`; keep the
   original `seedlings` object separate so that outputs from the two studies
   cannot silently overwrite each other.
2. Use `head()`, `tail()`, `dim()`, `names()`, and `str()` on the imported table.
   Record what each command establishes and what it does not. For example,
   seeing six rows in `head()` does not mean the dataset has six observations.
3. Check `length(transfer$plant_id)` and
   `length(unique(transfer$plant_id))`. The latter counts distinct identifiers.
   Compare them and explain why different counts would prompt investigation.
   Repeated IDs can be legitimate in a repeated-measurement design, so the study
   description—not a universal “duplicates are bad” rule—sets the expectation.
4. Inspect `unique(transfer$treatment)` and `table(transfer$treatment)`. Here
   `table()` counts the supplied labels. Check the expected group labels and
   nine records per group. Do not infer random assignment from the sorted row
   order; that information comes from the supplied study design.
5. Count missing initial and final lengths using `sum(is.na(...))`. Use
   `range(transfer$initial_mm)` and `range(transfer$final_mm)` to inspect minima
   and maxima. Range is a check on recorded values; it cannot determine the
   intended units or establish that every plausible number was measured correctly.
6. Make `reports/transfer-import-audit.txt` with the input path, dimensions,
   column types and roles, unique-ID count, group counts, missing-value counts,
   and units. State at least two things that required the data dictionary rather
   than a function call. Restart R and recreate the audit's numerical checks.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: use the object's actual column names

A column request such as `transfer$initial` is different from
`transfer$initial_mm`. Copy names from `names(transfer)` while learning. The
intended table is 18 rows by four columns, with 18 distinct IDs and no missing
initial/final readings. Matching these expectations helps identify the file but
does not replace understanding its measurements.
:::

## Independent transfer — inspect quantities in different units

Plan 60–90 minutes. The supplied `data/solutions.csv` table contains six simulated
calculation cases, not six independent treatment experiments. It lists solution
IDs, a solute name, mass in grams, molar mass in grams per mole, and final total
volume in millilitres. A mole is a unit of chemical amount; the supplied molar
mass converts grams to moles. You will inspect the input today, then use these
quantities in later calculation and report practice. No prior chemistry
knowledge is needed.

1. Import the table into `solutions` using a project-relative path. Before
   running `str()`, predict which columns should contain text and which should
   contain numbers. Compare the result with your prediction and explain why
   solution IDs and solute names are not measured quantities to average.
2. Check dimensions, unique solution identifiers, the two solute labels, and
   the absence or presence of missing values. Read Q01 aloud: 0.2922 g of sodium
   chloride, supplied molar mass 58.44 g/mol, final volume 100 mL. Identify the
   meaning and unit of every number before doing arithmetic.
3. Use `range()` on the numeric columns. Explain why the numbers for molar mass
   are not interchangeable with those for weighed mass, even though both types
   are numeric. A numeric storage type alone cannot authorise an operation.
4. Compare these two supplied vectors in a separate part of the script:
   `c(10, NA, 20)` and `c(10, 0, 20)`. Calculate their means and, for the first,
   the available-value mean using `na.rm = TRUE`. Record available and missing
   counts. Explain why using zero for an unavailable measurement invents evidence.
5. Save `reports/solutions-import-audit.txt` describing the table, its units,
   and what you could calculate from the supplied inputs. Include the formula
   in words if helpful: amount = mass / molar mass; concentration = amount /
   final volume in litres. This is not a request to operate laboratory equipment.
6. Ask a partner to run your saved inspection script from a fresh session.
   Have them identify which input generated each audit. If they see a table of
   24 plants where the note promises 18, investigate the filename/object choice
   before changing the note to match whichever result happened to appear.

**Check and retain:** `solutions.csv` has six rows, five columns, six unique IDs,
two supplied solute labels, and no missing inputs. The available-value mean of
10, NA, 20 is 15 from two observations; the mean of 10, 0, 20 is 10 from three.
Your two audit notes should preserve that distinction.


## Check your understanding

Why is the header not a plant? Why does the file's name not tell R the units?
Why should the script work from a classmate's project folder?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

The header labels columns rather than containing an observation. Units are
metadata supplied by people; R only sees column names and values. The script uses
relative paths and the same documented folder structure rather than your username.
There are no missing final lengths in the clean seedling dataset.
:::
